claims.text: Equimolar or nearly equimolar CoCrFeNiTi in a homogeneous simple solid-solution state has relatively low hardness and strength.
The low hardness and strength arise because the homogeneous solid solution provides minimal obstacles to dislocation motion.
The alloy has little effective lattice distortion beyond that associated with its constituent elements.
The starting material contains no significant precipitates or secondary phases.
Plastic deformation in the simple solid solution occurs mainly by facile dislocation glide and dynamic recovery.
The absence of precipitate or secondary-phase pinning limits the accumulation of strain hardening.
Limited strain hardening produces relatively low hardness and yield strength.
Facile glide and recovery impart favorable ductility and machinability.
A post-casting heat treatment can produce fine, evenly distributed precipitates or secondary phases in CoCrFeNiTi.
The as-cast single-phase alloy will have lower yield strength than a heat-treated precipitate-containing variant.
The as-cast single-phase alloy will have lower hardness than a heat-treated precipitate-containing variant.
The precipitate-containing variant will exhibit a higher strain-hardening rate than the as-cast single-phase alloy.
Post-deformation microscopy of the simple solid-solution alloy will show relatively mobile dislocation structures and signs of dynamic recovery.
Post-deformation microscopy of the heat-treated alloy will show precipitate-induced dislocation pinning.
The proposed mechanism applies to equimolar CoCrFeNiTi in a single-phase state under room-temperature deformation at conventional mechanical-test strain rates.
Formation of secondary phases or testing at temperatures that activate different deformation mechanisms may change the predicted behavior.

contradictions.description: The hypothesis describes a low work-hardening rate, whereas the predicted outcome calls the as-cast alloy's strain-hardening rate moderate. These descriptions are not necessarily mutually exclusive, but the intended magnitude is internally ambiguous.
